I don't understand how a stock buy back works. Were the executives and stock holders making money doing this? How? And if not, who did?

A stock buyback works like this:

*Company A is worth $1000 and has issues 100 shares. *Each share is worth $10. *Company A offers to buy up shares and purchases 10 shares back from the market. These shares are destroyed. *Each share is now worth $11.11.

Now consider this with companies worth billions of dollars and thousands, if not millions of shares on the market. In order to get to move that needle a little bit, the total pool of shares needs to decrease significantly. Sometimes this is worth it if the company wants to reduce the amount of stock on the market and reduce the amount of control that others have, reduce the amount of dividends which are paid out each year (dividends are an amount of money paid out to each share each year. Typically linked to profits, health of company, etc), or for other reasons).

Not only that, but sometimes people won't want to give up their shares and companies will offer a premium for the shares. Consider the example above: if Company A wanted to do it again, people might realize that the company wants to buy up shares and drive the price up. They may not sell for less than 13, 14, 15, or more dollars. This only works so well for so long, as the market is only willing to pay for what things are worth. Stock prices are usually linked to the health of the company- the higher they are, the better the company is doing. Typically.

Returning to the above example, if Company A did a buyback of 30 shares (spending $50 to do it) their share price is now $13.57 (950/70). However, if the company is evaluated later in the year as only being worth $750 due to bad investments, low profits, lawsuits, etc, the shares are only worth $10.71 (750/70). If the company only had $200 in liquid assets with which to conduct business, product development, etc, they burned a full quarter of what they had to use in the year and barely moved the needle at all. This is, in effect, what has happened with GE and GM, except that both companies also apparently borrowed money to increase the price of their stock.

As for cui bono? Anyone with stocks in either company would have profited up until the collapse. Executives typically have stock options- the ability to buy stock at a reduced price/from a specific pool of stock with fixed prices/etc, and stock holders get dividends or the ability to sell the stock at the higher price before it crumbles. Anyone who would have seen the writing on the wall or had knowledge ahead of time could have sold off the stocks before the bottom fell out.

I don't think these guys understand share buybacks.

Let's say you invested $10,000 in 1,000 shares of a stock at $10 each. The company made a profit, and paid out $1 in dividends per share that year. You then pay income taxes on the $1,000 your got through the dividend.

Let's say you invested $10,000 in 1,000 shares of a different stock at $10 each. The company made a profit, and instead of paying $1 in dividends that year, it spent the money buying back 1/10th of their outstanding stock. The stock, being rarer, increases in value to $11 per share. You sell 100 shares of the stock because you need the income, so you get back $1,100. You now pay capital gains taxes on the $100 profit instead of the higher income tax rate on the entire $1,000. Your remaining holdings, 900 shares at $11 each = $9,900, or about as much as you started out with. Alternatively, you could decide not to sell any stock, and now have $11,000 worth of stock and pay no taxes on it (yet).

This is the real reason many companies do stock buybacks rather than pay dividends. That GM's stock went down after the buyback isn't really germane. If GM blew too much money on the buyback, not holding back enough to keep itself solvent, it would be just as stupid as if it paid out too much in dividends instead.
